title: The widow's jar (1 Kings 17:8–16)
hook: a starving widow shares her last cake, and the flour doesn't run out

segments.voice: Yesterday, at Cherith, fed by ravens morning and evening, until the brook dried up. Your line was the ravens came. What help did you say yes to? Day seven hundred thirty-one.

A woman is picking up sticks at the gate of a town called Zarephath. Two sticks, the text says. Enough for one small fire. The brook has dried up, and the word has come to Elijah: go to Zarephath, "behold, I have commanded a widow woman there to sustain thee." Yesterday the ravens were commanded. Today it's a widow, and she doesn't seem to know it. Zarephath isn't in Israel. It belongs to Zidon, the country Queen Jezebel comes from. Elijah walks up, a stranger and a foreigner, and asks her for a little water. Then, as she turns to get it, for a piece of bread. Today, the widow's jar.

Her answer, in the King James Bible, is stark: "As the LORD thy God liveth, I have not a cake, but an handful of meal in a barrel, and a little oil in a cruse: and, behold, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go in and dress it for me and my son, that we may eat it, and die." Listen to one small word: thy God. Not mine. Yours. She is not of Elijah's people, and she expects this to be the last meal she and her son will eat. And Elijah says something that sounds outrageous: "Fear not; go and do as thou hast said: but make me thereof a little cake first." Me first. Then the promise: "The barrel of meal shall not waste, neither shall the cruse of oil fail, until the day that the LORD sendeth rain upon the earth." Everything turns on what she does next, and the text says it plainly: she went and did according to the saying of Elijah. She gives from her last, to a foreigner, on the strength of a promise from a God she calls his. And "the barrel of meal wasted not, neither did the cruse of oil fail." Look at what the miracle is, and isn't. The text never says the barrel overflowed. Nobody opens a bakery. The meal simply doesn't run out: "she, and he, and her house, did eat many days." Enough, not more. In Luke's Gospel, Jesus remembers her. There were many widows in Israel in that famine, he says, but Elijah was sent to none of them except this one, a widow in Sarepta, a city of Sidon.

Here's the practice: share a little from what's short. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you don't have much of right now: time, money, patience, energy. Notice how tightly you're holding it. Then bring to mind one person who could use a small piece of it. Not all of it. A handful. A phone call, a meal, an hour, a kind word when you're running low on kind words. Hold that small share in mind and picture giving it. If you pray, you can bring that person before God. The bell holds the time.
Zarephath. The town where a widow fed a stranger from her last handful, and the meal and oil were there each day, until the rain.
Your line: the jar did not fail. Today, give one small share from something you're short on, and watch whether you still have enough. Day seven hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Some Christians tell the story of the widow of Zarephath when they talk about generosity in hard times, and Jesus's mention of her in Luke 4 is sometimes read alongside it.

original.note: Hebrew: a jar or pitcher; the King James calls it a barrel of meal (1 Kings 17:12).

trapdoor: what you thought: a miracle about endless flour.
what it means: a foreign widow shares her last with a stranger, and there's enough each day, never more, until the rain.
what a scholar hears: she calls him 'the LORD thy God' (17:12), and in Luke 4:25–26 Jesus names her, a widow of Sidon, as the one Elijah was sent to.

Luke 4:25–26 is paraphrased. The index carry says 'jar'; the KJV says 'barrel of meal' and 'cruse of oil'. Kept the carry exactly; the script explains the KJV words.
